name: Hordeum
look_here_first: HORDEUM: on the central flowering SPIKE, look at ONE RACHIS NODE for THREE spikelets clustered together (middle usually fertile, two lateral often sterile). That TRIAD means BARLEY GENUS, not LITTLE BARLEY species. Native annual LITTLE BARLEY (*H. pusillum*) has short upright tight spike + relatively short straight glumes; native-to-Texas-at-state-scale FOXTAIL BARLEY (*H. jubatum*, COMPARISON ONLY) has usually perennial base, broad soft often nodding spike and very long outward-splaying glumes. ELYMUS wildryes have usually two MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets at a node.

recognition.where_to_look_first: HORDEUM: on the central flowering SPIKE, look at ONE RACHIS NODE for THREE spikelets clustered together (middle usually fertile, two lateral often sterile). That TRIAD means BARLEY GENUS, not LITTLE BARLEY species. Native annual LITTLE BARLEY (*H. pusillum*) has short upright tight spike + relatively short straight glumes; native-to-Texas-at-state-scale FOXTAIL BARLEY (*H. jubatum*, COMPARISON ONLY) has usually perennial base, broad soft often nodding spike and very long outward-splaying glumes. ELYMUS wildryes have usually two MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets at a node.
priority: 1 · TRIAD ANATOMY: expose intact ONE rachis node; middle fertile one-flowered spikelet + two often sterile lateral single-flowered spikelets.
2 · WHOLE SPIKE: little short erect tight 2–9 cm vs foxtail longer (~3–15 cm) often nodding and huge fluffy outspreading bristles.
3 · BARE BRANCH: little's outer glumes ~8–17 mm straighter/ascending; foxtail's glumes ~15–85 mm, strongly divergent bent at maturity, forming plume.
4 · LIFECYCLE: little ANNUAL rooted tuft vs foxtail usually PERENNIAL rooted bunch, stage/grazing complicate.
5 · ELYMUS KEY: wildryes 2 or more MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets per rachis node rather than 3 ONE-FLOWERED barley spikelets.
6 · LEAF COLLAR: little barley lacks auricles; common to foxtail too, so not a standalone split. Need true 1-mm glume and ligule macros.
recognition.warning: Foxtail barley H. jubatum is a comparison-only botanical source, not a new installed species. Do not mark introduced in Texas just because it is weedy; Kew places Texas within its native range, but local county certification is unreviewed. Maturity, drying, and hybrids can alter head appearance.

comparison_lesson.title: Little barley vs foxtail barley — first node, then glumes
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: LITTLE = small upright erect SPIKE + short straight GLUMES + ANNUAL. FOXTAIL = big nodding FEATHER + very long SPLAYED GLUMES + usually PERENNIAL. BOTH have 3 spikelets/node.
quick_split: Little barley H. pusillum — small native cool-season ANNUAL, narrow erect terminal spike (~2–9 cm), short nearly straight pale glumes (~8–17 mm) and relatively short lemma awns; three-one-flowered spikelet TRIADS.

Foxtail barley H. jubatum — comparison-only; normally PERENNIAL, foxtail-like nodding pale or purple-tinged head with dramatically outstretched long thin glumes (~15–85 mm in broad FNA); ALSO 3 spikelets per node.
Canada/Virginia WILDRYE (Elymus) — often two MULTIFLOWERED spikelets at successive spike nodes, rather than a Hordeum triad of one-flowered spikelets.
Introduced wall barley H. murinum — often more fanlike rachis-node cluster and developed auricles; verify glumes and actual floret morphology.
Cereal rye Secale cereale — a usually solitary multiflowered spikelet at each axis node; cultivated Hordeum vulgare is generally stouter but shares its genus arrangement.
comparison_lesson.science_guardrail: No new taxon admitted. Local foxtail nativity not screened; Kew state-level native in Texas. Do not use hairy bristle morphology alone to authorize removal or a plant native county claim.
field_sequence: FIRST: find the annotated SHORT narrow erect SPIKE and relatively close-lying AWNS on the existing little barley photo.

SECOND: in your local rooted plant, isolate ONE central rachis node—Hordeum has THREE grouped spikelets, a fertile middle and smaller lateral companions. This detail is NOT shown in the existing close enough for species-proof arrows.
THIRD: compare the foxtail photo below; mature Hordeum jubatum has MUCH longer glume awns spread broadly outward around a soft, often drooping head.
FOURTH: inspect the whole ROOTED base. H. pusillum is an annual; H. jubatum normally perennial. Photograph mature outer glumes with 1-mm ruler.
FIFTH: before calling it barley rather than wildrye, compare Elymus's MULTIFLORED paired spikelets. If structures cannot be resolved, use Hordeum sp. or Triticeae grass candidate.

comparisons.field_cues: LITTLE BARLEY: native North American short-lived cool-season grass with a compact, erect, bristly BARLEY spike. Each rachis node contains THREE closely grouped spikelets (central + two lateral), whose narrow awns form a small bottlebrush. Magnify one node to distinguish introduced foxtail barley or wall barley, and examine the annual rooted crown.
comparisons.lookalikes_and_split: Secale cereale also has a cereal spike but typically bears solitary paired-arranged spikelets (not Hordeum's distinctive triads) at rachis nodes; Hordeum murinum often has broader fanlike awned spikelet groups and is introduced. Cultivated barley Hordeum vulgare is larger and more robust; verify scale and individual spikelet arrangement.

what_to_teach_crew: Don't call the three spikelets per node a little-barley species trait: all examined Hordeum taxa share it.
Use whole plant and head size to orient, then measure outward glume divergence + life cycle.
Foxtail barley is a native North American species including Texas at state-scale; it can nevertheless be weedy. Do not equate weedy with exotic.
Use barley-vs-wildrye leaf collar/rachis node to avoid mistaking native Elymus in restored sites for lawn barley.
Awnlike outer glumes make much of foxtail's apparent beard; not every filament is a fertile lemma awn.
Choose genus-level identification and request fresh ripe spikelet macro rather than removing a possible native grass.
visual_needs: One intact local little barley flowering spike node under 10–20× showing 3 spikelets and fertile versus sterile florets, labels to real attached structures
Same plant short straight glumes and central lemma awn, measured on 1 mm scale
True auricle-free ligule and blade–sheath collar
Matched named foxtail barley H. jubatum adult rooted crown + splayed glumes from botanical voucher
Compare Elymus wildrye rachis with two MULTIFLOWERED spikelets at same scale; do not guess from photo silhouettes

items.caption: This image shows a patch with several short dense little-barley seed spikes, upright and often pale or tan at maturity. Learn the narrow, rather stiff habit. It does NOT show an individual spikelet triad, correct collar, or isolated rooted annual. Photo from Montana, not Hays.
items.why_it_matters: Gives crews a whole-patch recognition view of little barley's compact spring-to-early-summer seedheads, supplementing the closer original single-head image.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Exact Wikimedia Commons source with photo-level CC BY-SA 2.0 verified 2026-10-21; full 1000×750 source pixels inspected. One arrow to actual pale upright seedhead in the left-center region. No glume/triad/ligule annotations.

items.label: FOXTail BARLEY — long splayed awns make a broad feathery head (comparison only)
items.image_role: Actual CC BY-SA 2.0 Matt Lavin photo of ripe foxtail barley terminal spike; long bristles radiate strongly from a central axis
items.caption: Compare this broad, fluffy, often nodding foxtail-barley spike to the much shorter, compact, usually upright little-barley spike. Foxtail still shares Hordeum's THREE SPIKELETS per rachis node. The awn-spreading habit is visible; individual sterile vs fertile spikelets are not confidently resolvable from this view. Montana source, comparison-only.
items.why_it_matters: The WHOLE head silhouette is an efficient first split: H. jubatum bears dramatically long divergent bristles, while H. pusillum has shorter relatively erect ones. Always follow with intact nodes and rooted annual/perennial base.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Photo pixels viewed at 1000×750 via Wikimedia, one true head + long radiating awns. Gross arrows to visible regions only; not exact spikelet glumes or flowering-node anatomy. H. jubatum not a canonical installed species.

visual_comparison.overlay_note: No foxtail species installation; still one canonical H. pusillum. Existing source little barley arrows retained, foxtail gross/head arrows visually verified; true central fertile versus sterile lateral spikelets require a new 10–20× macro. Kew Texas native range for foxtail at STATE scale only, local status unreviewed. Second licensed Montana little-barley image inspected: multiple erect ripe heads; one actual gross seedhead arrow. No microscopic node triad visibility. Both source identities sourced, Hays-local photo gaps preserved.
